title: Equanimity
hookLine: the tenth perfection: balance in all conditions
tomorrow: how do you talk someone out of a bad idea without a fight?

lines: LOVED AT NOON. MOCKED BY FIVE.
cards: The group chat loves your post at noon. By five, someone has screenshotted it with a snarky caption. Same post.
Same you. Different weather. So how do you stay level?
The Buddha has a list for exactly this, and it's older than any feed: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. The eight worldly conditions, he calls them.
They spin after the world, he says, and the world spins after them.

teach.h: NOBODY GETS OUT OF THE WEATHER.
teach.b: Here's the surprise in that sutta: nobody gets out of the weather. The one who has heard the teaching and the one who hasn't both meet praise and blame. The difference is what happens next.

teach.h: IT COMES; IT'S SUBJECT TO CHANGE.
teach.b: When praise comes, the one who has heard reflects: this has come, and it doesn't last; it's subject to change. Blame gets the same reflection. And so neither one takes over the mind.
The Pali word is upekkha, equanimity: balance, an even mind. It isn't not caring. It's caring without being thrown.

teach.h: A ROCK NOT SHAKEN BY THE WIND.
teach.b: The Dhammapada gives it one picture, in Max Müller's translation: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." The wind still blows. The rock is still a rock.
Look at what that does with blame, the hard half. It doesn't wave blame away. A rock still hears the wind.

teach.h: TRUE BLAME: FIX IT. PRAISE: NO HOUSE.
teach.b: If the blame is true, fix the thing.
If it isn't, let it pass. Either way, it doesn't get to tell you who you are. And praise gets the very same treatment.
Enjoy it, say thanks, and don't build a house on it.

how: Theravada Buddhists chant the Mangala Sutta, whose blessings include a mind unshaken when touched by the ways of the world, and equanimity is practiced as one of the four divine abodes, with kindness, compassion and gladness.

o: a deep trance where you feel nothing at all
equanimity: an even mind in praise and blame
staying silent whenever someone criticizes you

p: two of the eight worldly conditions
fix the thing, then let it pass

s: it's caring without being thrown: check the blame, enjoy the praise, keep your balance.
the sutta says the wise meet praise and blame too
nobody gets out of the weather; the difference is what happens next.
praise is safe; only blame needs equanimity
the sutta treats both alike: it comes, it doesn't last, it's subject to change.

games.q: your sketch gets a pile of likes, then one stinging comment, and the comment is all you can think about. what does upekkha do?
o: check whether the comment is fair, keep what's true, let the rest pass.
delete the post, so the comment can't sting anymore.
reread the likes until the comment stops mattering.
games.why: upekkha doesn't wave blame away or hide behind praise. it checks what's true and lets the rest blow past, like wind on a rock.

practice: Take a pen. On one line, write a recent bit of praise; under it, a recent bit of blame, the same size, in the same calm hand. Read both once, slowly, and let them sit side by side, the way two kinds of weather share one sky.

wordCard.voice: Upekkha: equanimity, an even mind that stays itself through gain and loss, praise and blame.

orig.note: Pali: equanimity, an even mind (Sanskrit upeksha).

carryVoice: Your line: balance. A rock in the wind, the same at noon and at five. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.6, Lokavipatti Sutta (the eight worldly conditions; the instructed disciple reflects that they are impermanent and subject to change, so they do not take over the mind)

sources.q: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.

sources.ref: Buddhavamsa 2 (the ten perfections, ending with equanimity)
